definition: To make someone hostile or annoyed through your words or actions.
example: Raising the rent twice in one year antagonized even the most patient tenants.
nuance: To antagonize is to stir up hostility in someone else; to agonize is to suffer worry or anguish yourself.
prompt: A new manager needs the warehouse staff to accept an unpopular schedule change.
options: She explained the change calmly, careful not to antagonize the workers who disliked it.
The manager would antagonize for hours over which shift she should take herself.
To antagonize the staff, she thanked them warmly and offered everyone longer breaks.
She posted a short memo on the break room wall to antagonize everyone about the new start times.
reasons: Avoiding words that would turn already unhappy workers against her fits the term exactly.
Fretting over a personal choice is agonizing; the word needs someone who is being provoked.
Warm thanks and extra breaks soothe people, which is the reverse of stirring up resentment.
Simply informing people is neutral; the verb implies deliberately or carelessly creating ill will.

practice.prompt: Two neighbors have been arguing about the fence between their yards.
options: Leaving his trash cans on her side of the fence was sure to antagonize his neighbor.
His neighbor began to antagonize over whether the fence should be painted white or gray.
He hoped a plate of homemade cookies would antagonize her and end the dispute.
The fence was antagonized by years of rain until its boards began to warp.
reasons: An inconsiderate act during a dispute is likely to deepen her anger toward him.
Anxiously weighing paint colors is agonizing; no one here is being made hostile.
A friendly gift meant to settle a quarrel aims to calm her, not to provoke her.
The verb applies to people or animals roused to hostility, not objects worn down by weather.
